Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion Inside the manufactured water crisis in Tema, Gbetsile, Dawhenya and Community 25 Source : Sitsofe Mensah 21 October 2026 7:02am Audio By Carbonatix
When a state utility monopoly requires its paying customers to physically besiege a district office before management discovers that its distribution lines have been bone-dry for months, we are no longer witnessing an engineering challenge. We are witnessing institutional abdication.
On Tuesday, October 6, 2026, exasperated residents of Community 25 and neighbouring enclaves marched on the Ghana Water Limited (GWL) office in Gbetsile. For more than sixty days, their taps had yielded nothing but air. Formal letters had been written. Petitions had been lodged. Bureaucratic indifference met all of them, while families bled thousands of cedis every month buying water of questionable provenance from commercial tankers.
Two weeks after that protest, on October 20, GWL’s grand managerial response finally hit the newsstands: management had undertaken a "field visit" across Community 25, Tema, Ashaiman New Town, and Gbetsile to "assess the difficulties with water distribution, identify the factors affecting supply, and explore measures to improve service delivery"—culminating in the announcement of a "planned zoning system".
To any serious observer of infrastructure governance, that two-week sequence is a damning indictment of how Ghana runs—and regulates—public utilities. Water distribution is hydraulic physics, not a scavenger hunt. A utility does not need a street protest and a management convoy to discover that its own mains have been depressurised for sixty days."
Why should it take a customer revolt for utility executives to start by understanding the blockers in their own distribution network? Do the managers of GWL’s Tema Region and Gbetsile district no longer know which neighbourhoods they supply water to, at what pressure, and at what frequency?
Even without household smart meters, a minimally competent water utility operates on bulk flow meters, booster station logs, valve schedules, and pressure gauges across its District Metered Areas (DMAs). Every morning, operational logs tell district engineers how much treated volume leaves the plant and which distribution mains register zero flow.
Only two possibilities explain a utility management team putting on hard hats in late October to "discover" why communities have been dry since August:
In January 2026, GWL Managing Director Adam Mutawakilu made headlines by reassigning 41 managers nationwide, ostensibly to "crack the whip on poor performance". Nine months later, the dry pipes across Community 25, Ashaiman, Gbetsile, and Dawhenya prove that shuffling personnel chairs without fixing accountability or hydraulic capacity is mere theatre.
Even more insulting is the substance of GWL’s proposed mitigation. Management has touted a "planned zoning system" to help households plan their lives. Yet, in the same breath, GWL failed to publish the zone maps, name the specific communities assigned to each zone, state the pumping days, and provide an effective start date.
Meanwhile, on the ground, water still isn't flowing, and residents have been told plainly that no impactful engineering work has been done to address the supply deficit. Announcing a rationing schedule without dates, zones, or pipe pressure is not an engineering intervention. It is a public relations tranquilliser designed to demobilise angry residents. "On October 13, GWL dared to cite PURC's L.I. 2413 to threaten consumers over 'unauthorised changes in water use'—while brazenly violating Regulation 39 of that very same law by leaving entire communities dry without notice.
PURC’s Selective Amnesia: Fines for Power, Silence for Water?
If GWL’s posture is an insult to ratepayers, the silence of the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC) is a betrayal of its statutory mandate.
Homeowners Associations (HOAs) across these enclaves didn't just vent on social media; they followed the law and formally petitioned the regulator. Weeks later, what PURC is doing with those petitions under its governing statutes remains a closely guarded secret.
The law does not give PURC the luxury of being a passive spectator:
Here lies the rank hypocrisy. On October 13, 2026—while Community 25 and Gbetsile taps remained dry—GWL issued a national press release invoking L.I. 2413 to warn consumers against "unauthorised changes in water use". GWL remembers L.I. 2413 when policing citizens, but suffers amnesia regarding Regulation 39 when cutting off whole towns.
Worse still, PURC has a double standard. Ghanaians have not forgotten how PURC invoked Regulation 39 of L.I. 2413 to slap Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) board members with a GH¢5.86 million regulatory fine for failing to publish a load-shedding timetable and give prior notice of outages. Why is unannounced dumsor a finable statutory offence under L.I. 2413, while months of unannounced "dum-nsuo" across Tema, Gbetsile, Ashaiman, and Dawhenya elicit not a single compliance order or penalty from Dr Shafic Suleman’s Commission?
Every single quarter—most recently on September 24, 2026—PURC convenes with Swiss-watch precision to run macroeconomic models for its Quarterly Tariff Reviews. Why does that institutional efficiency vanish the moment Homeowners Associations petition the Commission to enforce quality-of-service rules?
Follow the money. Every week that piped infrastructure fails along the Community 25–Gbetsile–Dawhenya corridor, a lucrative secondary market of private water tankers booms. Where do those tankers draw the bulk water they retail to desperate households at extortionate rates? Frequently from GWL’s own hydrants and bulk filling points. When institutional failure feeds a profitable parallel economy—and triggers zero regulatory penalties—the urgency to fix depressurised residential mains mysteriously evaporates.
Ratepayers are done being placated by hard-hat photo opportunities and phantom zoning plans. If GWL management and PURC still serve the public interest, four actions are non-negotiable within the next seven days:
Until water flows through the pipes rather than through press releases, those in GWL's executive suites and PURC's regulatory chambers should know one thing: citizens are no longer buying the theatre.
